name: Jim Elliot
title: Jim Elliot: a missionary calling and the tragedy of 1956
description: Jim Elliot, the five missionaries killed in Ecuador in 1956, and why their story should be read with good sources and respect for the Waorani people.

sections.heading: Before the photograph and the memory
paragraphs: Jim Elliot was born in Portland in 1927 and studied at Wheaton College. In 1952 he traveled to Ecuador with Pete Fleming. There he began working among Kichwa communities before the attempt at contact for which he would become known. Language preparation and the daily life of the mission came before the episode that usually fills the accounts about him.

The letters preserved at Wheaton show that the Elliots kept in touch with churches that supported their work. The archive identifies the congregation in Williams, Oregon, as one of them. That documentation lets us see a mission sustained by correspondence, gifts and relationships, as well as by extraordinary events.

sections.heading: Five lives and an encounter that ended in death
paragraphs: Elliot, Pete Fleming, Ed McCully, Roger Youderian and the pilot Nate Saint took part in an attempt to reach the Waorani. Mission Aviation Fellowship describes exchanges of gifts from an airplane and the setting up of a camp beside the Curaray River. In January 1956, the five men were killed.

Missionary publications gave the event wide coverage. When reading them, it is wise to recognize their perspective: they tell of the loss from the point of view of the missionaries’ families and organizations. The Waorani people have their own history. Here their own name is used, rather than turning the old outsiders’ label “Auca” into a description of their identity.

reflection: In 2 Corinthians 4:5–7, Paul distinguishes the messenger from the Lord he proclaims and describes the frailty of those who carry that message. Elliot’s story can help us think about Christian self-giving from within that frailty. A missionary’s sacrifice calls for respect, but enthusiasm for his memory should go hand in hand with prudence and historical understanding.

For those who serve among other cultures, this account invites them to learn languages, to listen, to understand fears and to respect people. Christian mission needs patience and responsibility. The memory of an early death does not give license to reduce a whole community to a stereotype or to explain a tragedy with details the sources cannot confirm.
review_note: Letters and photos whose archive requires permission are not reproduced. No motives are invented for the attackers, and no final speeches.
